Case Vignette: "Joseph"

Joseph is a 47-year-old man, single, who has been working as a park ranger in a large national park for the past twelve years. He presents for evaluation at the urging of his supervisor, who noticed a marked decline in his ability to manage routine patrols and interactions with visitors. Joseph sits forward in his chair, his large frame coiled with tension, his eyes scanning the room as if cataloging exits.

He was born and raised in a small, rural village in a country that experienced a brutal civil war. When he was 22, he was a university student visiting his family during a holiday break when the conflict reached his home. He describes a night of relentless shelling and gunfire. He and his family hid in a root cellar beneath their home. He remembers the damp earth smell, the sound of his mother's whispered prayers, and the screams from the village. The next morning, he emerged to find his home and most of the village destroyed. He found his neighbor, an elderly man, dead in the street, his body partially covered by rubble. Joseph was the one who had to identify the body for the aid workers. He was not a soldier; he was a civilian caught in a place where war was the only reality.

After the ceasefire, he managed to leave the country and eventually immigrated to the United States. For years, he was functional. He worked hard, earned his degree in environmental science, and found solace in the quiet, predictable rhythms of the natural world. He thought the war was behind him.

But about six months ago, during a routine patrol, a visitor's car backfired. The sound was sharp, metallic. Joseph says he "lost time." He found himself on the ground, behind a fallen log, his heart hammering, his hands covering his head. He was drenched in a cold sweat and could not stop trembling. He could not recall the drive back to the station. Since that day, he has been unable to shake a feeling of pervasive dread.

In sessions, Joseph describes a constant state of hypervigilance. He cannot tolerate the sound of helicopters anymore-even the park's medevac chopper sends him into a panic. He avoids the eastern edge of the park, which is denser and reminds him of the forest near his village. He has stopped listening to music, because a sudden crescendo or a drum beat can trigger a flashback. He wakes three to four times a night, drenched in sweat, convinced he can hear shelling in the distance, only to realize it is the wind rattling his window.

His relationships have suffered. He has never married, and he now avoids the few friends he had. He feels disconnected, as if a pane of glass separates him from the world. He describes a pervasive guilt-not survivor's guilt in the classic sense, but a guilt that he survived by leaving, that he is here, safe, while the ghosts of his village remain. He alternates between a flattened, emotionless state and sudden, explosive irritability. Last week, he yelled at a family of hikers for straying off the trail, something he would have handled with gentle patience before.

He carries a small rock in his pocket. It is from his village. He says he does not know why he keeps it, but he cannot bring himself to throw it away. He holds it when the memories come. His PCL-5 score is 74, indicating severe PTSD symptoms. He is not sleeping. He is not eating. He is simply surviving, day by day, in a landscape that once healed him but now feels like a foreign and hostile territory.
